topStories.headline: $9.25 Million Philanthropic Gift Targets Persistent Trouble at Mission's BART Plazas
topStories.dek: The Crankstart Foundation's donation is the largest outside infusion of cash yet in a nearly two-year effort to calm 16th and 24th Street.
topStories.body:
Mayor Daniel Lurie and District 9 Supervisor Jackie Fielder announced Friday that San Francisco will receive a $9.25 million gift from the Crankstart Foundation to address poor street conditions at the Mission District's two BART plazas and the surrounding blocks. The plazas at 16th and 24th Streets draw more than 10,000 visitors daily, and persistent open-air drug use and disorder there have dogged Lurie's administration since he took office.

The gift arrives after nearly 20 months of city-led interventions — including a 90-day multi-agency enforcement surge, a bus-sized police command van parked on the southwest plaza around the clock, weekend stall markets, community ambassadors, and street outreach teams. The city also recently launched an online dashboard tracking citations, arrests, and 311 complaints at the plazas. Despite those efforts, neighbors have repeatedly said improvements are uneven, and overnight hours remain the city's biggest challenge at the site.

The Crankstart donation represents a new phase of outside investment in a problem that city government alone has not solved. What specific programs the money will fund has not yet been detailed publicly. Fielder, who represents the Mission, has previously pressed for 24-hour ambassador coverage at both plazas and pushed back on the idea that enforcement alone is a sufficient long-term answer.

Mission Local reported this week that the city has spent portions of the past year trying everything from pop-up markets meant to activate the plazas to deploying multi-agency teams capable of connecting people to drug treatment and shelter. The question city officials have yet to answer is how to sustain any visible improvement once temporary programs wind down.

topStories.headline: Voters Reject Prop I, Dealing Blow to Mission-Backed 'Social Housing' Measure
topStories.dek: The affordable-housing transfer-tax measure, championed by Mission progressives and fiercely opposed by real-estate money, lost 54–46 in Tuesday's election.
topStories.body:
San Francisco's Proposition I — the measure that would have dedicated half the revenue from the city's large-property transfer tax to affordable and cooperative 'social housing' — failed at the November 3 ballot, with roughly 54 percent of voters saying no and 46 percent in favor, according to results posted by the SF Standard and NBC Bay Area. The SF Department of Elections will not certify the final count until December 3.

The Mission District was the heart of the campaign to pass Prop I. Supporters argued the measure would funnel an estimated $120 million a year from taxes on real-estate sales over $10 million into affordable construction, homelessness prevention, and resident-controlled housing of the kind common in Vienna and Singapore but rare in American cities. The measure was written by former Supervisor Dean Preston, a tenants attorney and longtime Mission housing advocate.

Opponents, led by the city's major real-estate interests, raised more than $2.7 million against the measure — the largest sum spent against any proposition on the November ballot. Mayor Lurie's campaign characterized the fund as a 'slush fund,' even though Lurie's own office would have controlled the money under the measure's text.

Tuesday's broader results continued a rough night for Mission-area progressives. Scott Wiener won the congressional race to succeed Nancy Pelosi, defeating Mission-area favorite Connie Chan. Mayor Lurie's three City Charter reform measures passed handily. For tenant and housing advocates in the neighborhood who have watched displacement accelerate for years, the defeat of Prop I was a significant setback.

topStories.headline: 24th Street BART Elevator Was Broken for 94 Days. Was That Even Legal?
topStories.dek: Mission Local's investigation found the station's only street-level elevator has been out of service for a total of 98 days this year — raising questions about BART's 2024 accessibility settlement.
topStories.body:
The elevator connecting street level to the 24th Street Mission BART station's concourse — the only one of its kind at that plaza — was taken out of service on July 13 for emergency repairs to an aging hydraulic jack and tank. Despite an initial promised return date of August 10, the elevator did not come back online until October 15: 94 days after the outage began. Water intrusion in the underground work site was given as one reason for the extended delay.

Mission Local reported this week that since January, the same elevator has been out of service for a cumulative 98 days — meaning wheelchair users and others who depend on it have been unable to use the 24th Street station for roughly one-third of the year. BART acknowledged that repairs did not take place every day during the outage.

The extended failure raises legal questions. In 2024, BART settled an accessibility lawsuit and agreed to fix or modernize 75 elevators across its network. According to documents obtained by Mission Local, the 24th Street elevator appears on BART's own 'elevator modernization prioritization 2026' list, suggesting the agency was already aware of its fragile condition before the July emergency. BART has not publicly confirmed whether the duration of the outage put it in violation of the settlement terms.

For daily riders — particularly seniors, people with disabilities, and families with strollers navigating one of the Mission's busiest transit hubs — the months-long outage was more than an inconvenience. BART's guidance during the closure was to use the 16th Street Mission or Glen Park stations instead.

moreNews.headline: Adobe Books Hit by Paint Vandal Three Times in Six Days
moreNews.body: Adobe Books, the cooperatively run used bookstore and community arts space at 3130 24th St. in the Mission, was vandalized with red paint for the third time in six days as of October 30. The first incident occurred on Sunday, October 25; the storefront was struck again by Friday, and hit once more that same Thursday morning. San Francisco Public Works crews were called to clean up paint from the sidewalk and storefront. The bookstore's workers told Mission Local they were mystified about who might be responsible. No arrest had been reported as of publication.

moreNews.headline: Bernal Heights Commercial Building Fire Displaces Eight on October 28
moreNews.body: A one-alarm fire at a commercial building in the 900 block of Peralta Avenue in Bernal Heights displaced eight occupants in the early morning hours of Wednesday, October 28, according to the San Francisco Fire Department. Firefighters battled the blaze near the Alemany Farmer's Market for one hour before containing it. No injuries were reported, and the American Red Cross assisted the displaced residents. The cause of the fire had not been released as of initial reporting.
